title: Shema, from the right
hookLine: Hebrew is read from right to left
carry: kavanah: slow words, a listening heart

lines: THE LINE STARTS AT THE RIGHT.
cards: Hand a Hebrew prayer book to someone who's never held one, and watch their hands. They open it the usual way and land on the last page. They flip, frown, flip again.

Then someone leans over, smiling, and turns the whole book around. The spine goes on the right. The first page sits where an English book would end, and its first line starts at the right-hand margin.
Nothing is backward. It's just facing the other way.

teach.h: THE BOOK OPENS FROM THE RIGHT.
teach.b: Hebrew is written and read from right to left: the pen starts at the right margin and travels left, and the eye follows. Second, the book.
Because each line runs leftward, the binding sits on the right and pages turn from left to right. A Hebrew book begins where an English one ends. Third, one word, slowly.

Take the line you first met in your second week, said by tradition morning and night, from Deuteronomy: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew the first word is Shema, three letters.
On the far right, shin, with its three arms. To its left, mem. Then ayin.
Shin, mem, ayin: Shema. Read the other way, it falls apart. Fourth, why it matters for a beginner.
Eyes trained left to right have to slow down here; they want to jump the wrong way. That slowness isn't a problem to fix. It's a doorway.
You can't skim a language you read against your habits, and attention in prayer is something the rabbis prize.

teach.h: KAVANAH: SLOW WORDS, A LISTENING HEART.
teach.b: They call it kavanah. So let the eye start on the right, and let it take its time.

how: Hebrew is written and read from right to left, so Hebrew books and prayer books open from the right; children learning to read trace words from the right margin, often starting with familiar words like Shema.

games.why: you can't skim a line you read against your habits. the rabbis prize kavanah, the heart attending to each word, and slow eyes make room for it.

practice: Rest a finger on the table and start at the right: draw shin, three small arms rising from a base, then mem to its left, a box open at the bottom left corner, then ayin, two short strokes meeting in a tail that drops below the line.
Trace the same path once more, slowly, right to left, and say the word softly as you finish: Shema. If you pray, it's the word that opens the Shema.

wordCard.voice: Right to left. The way Hebrew runs: from the right margin, from the right side of the book, one slow word at a time. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear. Three letters, read right to left: shin, mem, ayin.
